notes.text: This word is probably also to be reconstructed as the original form underlying the various forms found in the Palestinian Targum tradition paralleled by the form in PsJon at Gen 50:1. Interestingly enough, the sole Syriac example preserves the correct vocalization although the consonantal spelling is incorrect (though one suspects rather an error by Budge here!). citations.translation: a bedecked building for a theater from the Aegean realm [~MT בַּת־אֲשֻׁרִים מֵאִיֵּי כִּתִּיִּם]

notes.text: It is not clear that this is an adj. rather than a GN. Levy Ch-W p. 1:54 suggests Apollonia (Lycian/Byzantine city on the Antalyan coast), while the edition known to the Aruch reads איטליא i.e. Italy, here, perhaps as an explanation of Apulia. Given that it is for the ceiling of a theater, perhaps we should read a form of Africa (i.e. אפרקא or the like, as a source of impressive-looking wood. On the other hand, the Peshitta at 2Chron 1:17 renders Biblical Que, i.e. the Neo-Hittite state centered at Adana in the Cilician plain, as אפליא, so an Anatolian location should not be excluded. As for Apulia, it still has many ancient forests.

text.text: אי דבלא איהו לא מינטר פשיטא אלא דבלא איהו מינטר

citations.translation: if it is not guarded without him, that is obvious, but it is guarded without him

notes.text: Normally only as subject. Often it has the same extra semantic force as does hwyw, i.e. "he himself, he is the one who" and this was clearly understood in the LJLA tradition where it is found only as a subject. The etymology has long been debated, but we are convinced that it is of the same basic type as the repeated form hwyw with vocalic dissimlation and loss of initial heh. What remains unclear, however, is how many LJLA examples are simply due to scribal change toward the standard JBA usage, as clearly happened in the language of the Zohar. We suggest that any example without a clear emphatic function may well be the result of such a change, for in almost all such cases variant texts have simple הוא.

text.text: מטול דעל מיחמי כל עמא איתיקר

notes.text: For the sole JPA occurrence of this JBA and LJLA form compare the note s.v. mṭwl prep. In LJLA such spellings instead of simple מטול can occasionally be scribal "improvements" ; however, in TgChron (always) and other LJLA texts (mostly) there seems to be a clear distinction between this form used in the sense of "on behalf of" and מטול othewise, i.e., with very few exceptions the two forms are suppletive, with this form being used with pronominal suffixes and before the names of persons or groups, while מטול rarely occurs in such a context. Note that in Mandaic this form is found in the later manuscripts, while the early epigraphic texts use mṭwl.

notes.text: Forms with nun are found in Biblical Aramaic, Qumran, and Mandaic, i.e. the Official Aramaic Literary tradition; those without nun in JLA (> Samaritan, see Tal), Syriac, and Galilean. LJLA has both forms, but the evidence suggests an original attempt in that dialect to distinguish between the two, where nun-minus forms are meaning 1, those with nun meaning 2. Also note that this word is used exclusively in the targumic tradition for the literal meaning of ”fruit.” In those cases where the biblical text uses פרי in figurative senses such as “produce, offspring, results” and the like, the parallel targums regularly use other terms, in particular the cognate פירי. The etymological relationship between this word and Syriac ܗܒܒܐ "flower" is unclear. For the probable connection with Hebrew עֵנָב "grape" via Akkadian inbu see The Akkadian Influences on Aramaic, Assyriological Studies 19 (Chicago: Oriental Institute, 1974)')" onmouseout="toolTip()">AIOA

notes.text: See also s.v. Ɂdrkh; the forms are regularly confused in the manuscripts, with this form found in Geonic texts and the other in the Talmud. DJBA attempts to disambiguate them, claiming that this form is the "power of attorney" while the attested form is a scribal error based on the regular JBA afel of qwm which itself is often found in LJLA texts. In fact, though, aside from this unique substitution, it is a replication of the Syriac text (with verb-final nun omitted, while the initial nun is the Syriac 3mpl. verbal prefix. Thus, the insertion of this Hebrew lemma in some versions of the text may be ascribed to a copyist who read it as Hebrew.

notes.text: Etymologically speaking, איניש is simply an alternative spelling of the literary form איש (Ɂinš) and is not the same word as Ɂĕnāš, though it is an ancient development from the same root and shares both its semantics and syntagms (see s.v. Ɂnš). Others take it to be a direct phonetic development from Ɂnāš, a position we find difficult to justify. The confusion in JBAmb is complete, where both the pronominal (i.e. absolute state) and nominal (i.e. emphatic state, pl., construct) usages may be spelled אינש. Note that this word need not refer to a human being.

formsNote: JLAtg abs. (under stress?!) also אָב (i.e, with Hebrew!); Pl. Ɂăḇāhān, Ɂăḇāhāṯā; Syr. also ܐܲܒ̈ܵܗܸܐ and so almost always before suffixes; sg. w. pro. suffs.: Ɂăḇū-. A common LJLA (from PTA?) form shows imālā: איבא. In CPA some forms are written with the emphatic "p" instead of "b". At Mk 14:36( [ed. Kiraz), etc., the form ܐܲܒܒܿܵܐ is a transcription of the Greek rather than reflecting the Syriac, which does not double the beth. Rather the doubling of the beth in the emphatic sg. form is a distinctive feature of Western Aramaic. Indeed in Syriac poetry the initial vowel of the emphatic may be elided metri causa.

notes.text: See Nöldeke, CSG 148f. For the Syriac usage as copula:, A. Wertheimer, JSS 47(2002):1ff. As she points out, the copulative usage was undoubtedly influenced by Greek, but often appears in translated texts even where the Greek does not use the verb "to be"! It must be seen as a natural development of the kind of usage found already in Standard Literary Aramaic (Biblical Aramaic (Daniel!), JLA) with participles and other adjectives, i.e., where the existential nature of the predication is still paramount. In Syriac the participle is no longer nominal, hence Ɂīṯ is not used with it, only enclitic pronouns. A more comprehensive study still needs to be done, though.

notes.text: This rare lexeme is better known from the Rabbinic Hebrew examples (see Jastrow, pp. 13f.) where it means "to store up". The Mandaic and LJLA usages have been connected here because of their usage only with "words" and "speech". The semantic development, already partially attested in Biblical Hebrew, would seem to be "to labor in a field" > "to collect produce" > "to store up" > "to lock away".

notes.text: In a lengthy note, DJBA proposes that the root is Ɂzdy; he also rejects Friedman's suggestion that this root is simply a by-form of Ɂzl. Friedman is almost certainly correct, however. That "the l-d interchange is not found otherwise in JBA" is irrelevant. Common words regularly undergo uncommon phonological changes, and the regular changes undergone by this root in neo-Aramaic -- as well as the well_known assimilation of the /l/ to the /z/ in Eastern Syriac itself -- demonstrate its proclivity for such changes. In talmudic language, though, this colloquial form of אזל seems to have been limited to a specific semantic realm, while in other contexts the more literary אזל is usually still written (but often simply אזא, as in Syriac pronunciation), although many exceptions occur in the prints and manuscript sources. Almost certainly, though, mng. 1 was connected by its users with the earlier BIblical Aramaic Ɂzd "certain", said of a "word". Note Rashi's commentary to Daniel 2:8 where he renders אזדא as הלך.

notes.text: This is a common form from Mishnaic Hebrew (see Jastrow pp. 89f.), itself apparently a corruption of an otherwise unkown Greek word combining the words for "star", i.e. astro- with "knower", i.e., gnō. Levy’s proposed etymology ὁ στεγανος makes little sense in the contexts. Note that all the other versions use the standard Aramaic word for "sorcerer", i.e., ḥrš in these passages. Apparently PsJon wanted to use a foreign-sounding word to reflect the obviously foreign word in BH, but more importantly wanted to distinguish between the dream interpreting function of the Hebrew term in the Genesis passages, for which he uses the standard חרש, and the magical actions here.

notes.text: Forms such as this present a lexicographical problem. In JLA and LJLA they are simply standard verbal nouns of the derived conjugations and in all of the examples attested for this particular verbal noun used as a gerund without exceptional meaning. However, in JPA the normal derived stem infinitive is prefixed with mem, hence it is hard to claim that it is a simple v.n. in such cases (even if the form might be a loan from an underlying JLA ur-text!) hence the status as independent noun in such cases in DJPA. What, however, is the absolute form of such nouns? In standar JLA, LJLA grammar they end in final /ā/, not /ū/ as DJPA would have it. But there are a few cases of /ū/ attested. תיקו!

notes.text: In Syriac biblically-based sources, Edom and Edomite are normally substituted for Aram and Aramaean. It is probable that Mandaic references also imply Romans although that usage within Rabbinic Jewish texts, albeit regular, appears first only from the end of the tannaitic period. The motivation for the Rabbinic identification is complex; for which see most recently M. Hadas_lebel, Jerusalem against Rome (Peeters, 2006). For possible examples in Mandaic see s.v. dwmy adj.

formsNote: JLA, JBA a/i; Syr. a/a. In Syriac and Babylonian the lamadh is often retro-assimilated to zayin when there is no separating vowel in the form, presumably reflecting a more colloquial form, since such is always the case in spoken Eastern Aramaic. Rarer in JBA is the loss of final lamedh in forms with /ē/ in the second syllable, e.g.זי "go!", and the assimilation of the zayin to the lamedh, e.g.אלינן "we go".

notes.text: From: William Smith, A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, John Murray, London, 1875: ÁRTABA (ἀρτάβη), a Persian measure of capacity, principally used as a corn-measure, which contained, according to Herodotus (I.192), 1 medimnus and 3 choenices (Attic), i.e. 51 choenices = 102 Roman sextarii = 12 3/4 gallons nearly; but, according to Suidas, Hesychius, Polyaenus (Strat. iv.3, 32), and Epiphanius (Pond. 24) only 1 Attic medimnus = 96 sextarii = 12 gallons nearly: the latter is, however, only an approximate value. p138. There was an Egyptian measure of the same name, of which there were two sorts, the old and the new artaba (Didymus, c19). The old artaba contained 4 1/2 Roman modii = 72 sextarii = 9 gallons nearly, according to most writers; but Galen (c5) makes it exactly 5 modii. It was about equal to the Attic metretes; and it was half of the Ptolemaic medimnus, which was to the Attic medimnus as 3 : 2. The later and more common Egyptian artaba contained 3 1/3 modii = 53 1/3 sextarii = 6 1/2 gallons about,a which is so nearly the half of the Persian, that we may fairly suppose that in reality it was the half. It was equal to the Olympic cubic foot. (Rhemn. Fann. Carmen de Pond. et Mens. v.89, 90; Hieron. Ad Ezech. 5; Böckh, Metrolog. Untersuch. pp242, &c., 285; Publ. formsNote: OA construct: Ɂšt; OfA also Ɂn$h (i.e. Ɂanṯā). Up until Middle Aramaic the nun is always written and so still in Syriac where it is not pronounced and, as in other dialects, then assimilated to the taw (i.e. a radical consonant atuat (perhaps always as a pejorative); JBAmb also יתתא Plural nəšīn, nəšayyā, Syr. ܢܸܫܼ̈ܝܢ܂ ܢܸܫܹ̈ܐ; The original fem. marking taw should be spirantized, but apparently was not so in all dialects, leading, for example to the spelling of the emphatic form with a single taw in some JBA texts; The initial (originally short /a/) vowel of the singular form becomes /i/ in the closed syllable in Jewish dialects and Mandaic but remains /a/ in Syriac (also rarely in Mandaic). Mand. pl. apparently also ainšia, hence confused with the plural of Ɂnš.

notes.text: DJBA "a rush" following the usage of the cognate Akkadian word. We have interpreted the sole example cited there as belonging with Ɂšl "rope," but given the Akkadian parallel cited there, it could belong here, or the Akkadian example could be misinterpreted in the CAD! See also the extended discussion in Levy, s.v. The gaonic commentary cited by DJBA would seem to mean "bed shavings". That the Biblical Hebrew word was no longer understood by late rabbinic times in Eretz Israel is clear from the targumim to Gen. 21:33 (and other rabbinic treatments: see Hayward, JJS 49(1998):24ff.), thus the Targum Jonathan examples should be understood to be a Hebraism.

notes.text: See also s.v. Ɂyš, Ɂynyš and note that the latter is not the same word as this. (Technically this word is a second millennium BCE back-formation from the plural of the segholate noun *Ɂinš.) Note in particular that the absolute form refers to "person, somone" whereas the determined form more generally to mankind (at least after OfA). See also s.v. br Ɂnš, the more common usage. See, too, discussions s.vv. Ɂnšh, Ɂnšy bytɁ, Ɂynyš, Ɂnwš. The use of the absolute vs. the emphatic form is a distinctive marker of the difference between JLA targumim and latest LJLA material respectively, for which see Gottlieb (2020): p. 36.
